item.title: Amami Oshima Island — Guide
item.description: Amami Oshima, a large subtropical island in the seas between Kyushu and Okinawa (part of Kagoshima), is a paradise of natural beauty recognised as a UNESCO World Heritage site for its unique biodiversity. Ringed by white-sand beaches, coral reefs and clear turquoise seas ideal for swimming, snorkelling, diving and kayaking, its interior holds lush subtropical laurel forests and mangroves that are home to rare endemic species, including the elusive Amami rabbit, found nowhere else on earth.

item.title: Aoshima Island — Guide
item.description: Aoshima is a small, subtropical island just off the coast of Miyazaki city, connected to the mainland by a footbridge and famous for its natural beauty and romantic shrine. The little island is entirely covered in a lush jungle of some 5,000 betel palms and subtropical plants, giving it an exotic, southern-island feel. Ringing the island is one of its most striking features: the ‘Oni no Sentakuita’ or ‘Devil’s Washboard’, vast wave-cut platforms of ridged rock that radiate out into the sea in remarkable regular corrugations, exposed at low tide.

item.title: Shingu Beach and the Genkai Coast — Guide
item.description: North of Fukuoka city, the town of Shingu sits on the coast within the Genkai Quasi-National Park, a protected stretch of the scenic Genkai Sea coastline known for clean beaches, pine groves and offshore islands. Shingu’s beach is a pleasant, relatively uncrowded spot for a seaside stroll or a summer swim, backed by pines and looking out over the sea. From Shingu’s port, a short ferry runs to Ainoshima, a tiny fishing island famous as a ‘cat island’, where a large population of friendly cats roams the sleepy harbour and lanes — a quirky, popular half-day trip for animal lovers.

item.title: Tanegashima Space Center — Guide
item.description: Tanegashima, a long, flat subtropical island south of Kagoshima, is home to the Tanegashima Space Center, Japan’s largest rocket launch complex and often called one of the most beautiful launch sites in the world for its stunning coastal setting. Operated by JAXA, the Japanese space agency, it launches large rockets carrying satellites and cargo into space. Visitors can tour the vast grounds — set among white-sand beaches, blue seas and green headlands — and explore the free Space Science and Technology Museum, with displays on rockets, satellites, space exploration and a real rocket and equipment on show, plus guided tours of the launch facilities (by reservation).

item.title: Naoshima Art Island, Kagawa: The Complete Visitor's Guide
item.description: Naoshima is a small island of roughly 8 square kilometres in the Seto Inland Sea, about 50 minutes by ferry from Takamatsu. In the early 1990s, it was a quiet island with an ageing fishing population, a modest industrial presence, and no particular reason to appear on any travel itinerary. Over the following three decades, the Fukutake Foundation — the philanthropic arm of Benesse Holdings, based in Okayama — transformed it into one of the world’s most celebrated destinations for contemporary art and architecture.

item.title: Naoshima Art Island Japan Complete Guide 2026
item.description: Naoshima Art Island Japan Complete Guide: The Ultimate Insider’s Guide to Japan’s Living Art Museum If someone told you that a sleepy fishing island in the Seto Inland Sea would become one of the most important contemporary art destinations on the planet, you’d probably raise an eyebrow. But that’s exactly what happened to Naoshima — a tiny island of roughly 3,000 residents in Kagawa Prefecture, Shikoku — where world-class architecture by Tadao Ando, installations by Yayoi Kusama and James Turrell, and an entire village transformed into living art galleries have created something utterly unlike anything else in Japan, or the world.
